#3368. The Teenagers Taking a Cancer Drug to Get Taller

O ne video led to another until eventually my TikTok feed was full of teenagers trying to get taller. They were calling it “heightmaxxing,” a subset of the much-dissected world of “looksmaxxing,” where young men trade strategies for improving their appearance in hopes of warding off a fate of despair and loneliness. For these young men, the logic is mercilessly efficient: Everything in life is better if you’re tall.

The videos arrived with the narrative progression of a course syllabus. First came explainers on “heightism,” or discrimination based on someone’s height. Dating was a frequent point of frustration, with being tall treated as a prerequisite for being considered at all.

Then, slowly but surely, strategies on what you can do about it.

Eventually, I was watching teenagers discuss something called erda. They posted updates on how much they’d grown and compared notes on side effects. Some showed tape measures against marks on a wall; others labeled videos by how many days they’d been taking it. Erda, it turns out, was short for erdafitinib, a cancer drug that the boys on my feed believed could make them taller, pointing to reports of unexpected growth in children being treated for cancer. They were willing to endure debilitating symptoms to find out.

About half an hour into my conversation with Zak, a 17-year-old TikToker in New York, he tells me he had been preparing for the possibility of a hospital stay. He’d been taking erda on and off since he was 15, and after bouts of joint pain and nosebleeds, he expected that something might eventually go wrong. “I was literally saving money every single day. I was putting money aside from my work and everything just for a medical bill from erda.” He says he bought the drug from overseas online vendors, initially paying $300 for a month’s supply.

Zak says height became particularly important to him as he spent more time on social media. He remembers videos of women discussing how tall a man needed to be for them to consider dating them. At school, he says he was made fun of for being shorter than girls in his class. “I don’t like other people towering over me, and I don’t like having to look up to people,” he says. “I don’t know how to put it, but it feels like I’m not in control.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Erdafitinib, sold under the brand name Balversa, was first approved in 2019 to treat certain advanced bladder cancers in adults. Doctors have also used it off-label in clinical trials of children with rare cancers of the central nervous system. The drug’s known side effects are nothing short of gnarly: its prescribing information lists diarrhea, pain in the limbs, nausea, and nails separating from their nail beds, as well as excess phosphate in the blood, which can cause mineral deposits in soft tissues.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Johnson & Johnson, which markets Balversa, expressed concern about online content appearing to show young people using prescription drugs for unapproved purposes or without medical supervision. “It has not been approved to increase height, and its safety and effectiveness have not been established for that purpose or for use in any children or adolescents,” they said, adding that the company urges patients to consult qualified health professionals about treatment and to only use medicines from verified sources under medical supervision.

Zak reports nosebleeds, severely dry skin, and pain that made ordinary movements difficult. “Stretching my arm felt like my wrist was going to tear off,” he says. “Waking up, it felt like my spine was bent. I had to spend one hour of just stretching so my spine feels better.” Even then, he says, the pain persisted.

When we talk, he’s stopped taking the drug, though he’s ultimately pleased with the results and is already thinking about starting again. By his own measurements, he says he grew several inches between roughly ages 15 and 17, while taking erda on and off. He says his height had previously plateaued. Related Content Clavicular Can't Seem to Stay Out of Trouble: A List of His Controversies Are Clavicular’s Followers Rethinking His Influence? I Paid $49 for Clavicular’s ‘Looksmaxxing’ Academy. What I Saw Should Scare Us All Character.ai Was Sued Over a Teen's Suicide. It Just Banned Minors From Chatting With Bots

Adalbert Raimann, a pediatric endocrinologist at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria, is an author of an erdafitinib study often cited by heightmaxxers. Published online in July 2024 in the peer-reviewed journal Hormone Research in Paediatrics, it described unexpected growth in two children with central nervous system tumors.

Raimann explains that, during puberty, growth takes place in cartilage near the ends of bones, known as growth plates. Those plates fuse once we reach our full height, around early adulthood. Erdafitinib blocks proteins called fibroblast growth factor receptors. One of them, FGFR3, normally helps limit bone growth; blocking it can allow growth to speed up while the plates are still active.

Over video chat, Raimann stresses that why those children were receiving the drug matters. Doctors were trying to keep children with rare, life-threatening cancers alive after other treatments had failed. That meant using a drug not approved for children and tolerating serious side effects.

“And those receptors we’re targeting with erda, they’re present in basically every cell,” he says. “So we have no idea, not in adults and especially not in kids in this developing system, what we are doing in five to 10 years.”

After those growth plates have fully closed, Raimann says, there’s no way to naturally grow taller. It’s why some adults in the heightmaxxing world turn to dangerous and excruciating leg-lengthening surgeries, which involve cutting the leg bones and gradually pulling the sections apart so new bone grows in the gaps. It’s also why the demographic hungry for experimental treatments skews so young. The teenagers I spoke with felt like it was potentially their last chance to intervene.

For James, a 17-year-old on the West Coast who asks that I use only his first name, an X-ray helped set off his search for something that could make him taller. During our Zoom call, he holds up a translucent plastic container where he keeps the powder he identifies as erda. Then he brings his hand toward the webcam, curling his fingers to show me his fingernails. They’re yellowish and oozing pus. He says they’ve been falling off. “Bro, it’s bad.”

“I just thought I was just going to be a late bloomer because my uncles and dad, they grew very late,” he says. “So I got a bone-scan X-ray and yo, the doctor said I have a bone age of 18. I can maybe grow another millimeter. And I was five foot five, so it was pretty bad. So then I just knew that there had to be something that could make me taller.”

He says he began taking erda in late August and grew roughly two and a half to three inches in two months, while also using other drugs. “I grew more in two months than I did in one year,” he says.

Erda wasn’t the first drug James had considered. Doctors already prescribe growth hormone to help some children gain height, supplying a hormone the body naturally produces. Andrew Dauber, a pediatric endocrinologist at Children’s National Hospital in Washington, D.C., says there’s a distinction between treating a hormone deficiency and intervening because a child is just short.

“There are children who are deficient in growth hormone, who have severe growth issues, who really medically need growth hormone as indicated. And then there’s this gray zone of using growth hormone for short stature,” he says. The FDA also approves it for some children whose short stature has no identified cause, a category called idiopathic short stature. Dauber describes the threshold as “a height below minus 2.25 standard deviations.” This translates to an adult male height of five feet three and an adult female of four feet 11.

Though guidelines are set by the FDA, doctors have the option of prescribing growth hormone off-label for individuals who they think could benefit from it. The decision involves an expensive treatment with risks, Dauber says, and doctors disagree about when it is warranted.

“I’ve spoken to a lot of pediatric endocrinologists and some say, ‘Listen, I know they’re going to get it. They’re either going to get it off the internet or they’re going to go see a doctor who doesn’t know as much about it, and I feel like I should just give it to them and at least monitor them for safety and do it in a safer way,’” he says. “And then there are many endocrinologists who feel like this is not really a disease or not really a medical problem.”

Dauber says he has now received his first patient inquiry about erda. He will not prescribe it for growth. “That’s way too dangerous. We only know about it at the chemotherapeutic doses,” he says, referring to the amounts used to treat cancer.

James says that when he was younger, his parents refused to let him take growth hormone. After an endocrinologist told him he was nearly done growing at five foot five, he says, their guilt over that decision made them more permissive about his experiments with erda and other drugs. “They kind of let me do everything,” he says.

Zak says his parents “don’t approve of anything I’m doing.”

Both say that nothing would stop them from trying anything they can to get taller. “There’s this life that I have in mind, and I just want it so badly that I’m not going to let some risk stop me from getting the life I want,” James says. “I don’t know. I just want it so badly.”

There’s been a marked turn toward DIY healthcare in recent years, as alternative medicine and biohacking protocols gain mainstream popularity. People on social media increasingly promote injectable peptides and other invasive methods for optimizing one’s health and looks. For Zak, the adverse reactions have become part of that pursuit. “If I get into side effects, nobody would want to touch this compound,” he says. “But to me, I get obsessed over this stuff, and I still think it was worth it.”

James calls his bedroom a lab. He says he sources the drugs through black-market online suppliers. In addition to erda and human growth hormone, he says he’s experimented with tamoxifen and letrozole, two drugs used to treat breast cancer, and abaloparatide, a drug for osteoporosis. He also uses experimental compounds called SAG 21K and KY19382, which researchers have studied in mice for their effects on bone repair or growth.

He says he went to the hospital with a stomach bleed during his first month of taking erda, though he isn’t sure which exact compound caused it. He has since switched to online school because he says the pain and vomiting made attending in person too difficult. “At school, I threw up blood one time,” he says. “And it hurt so bad to move. I can only go out once a week. I just go out on Fridays and just rest the whole day because everything I’m doing, it makes me so tired and hungry that I literally just have to lay down.” He says his bones feel like they’re stretching apart. “So it’s hard to do anything.”

The anxiety around male height isn’t exclusively coming from the teens themselves. Both Raimann and Dauber say they regularly see parents looking for ways to help their child reach a particular height, especially the parents of young boys. “I had a mother say in front of her child, her teenage son, ‘If he ends up five-seven, his life is over,’” Dauber recalls. “My eyes just shot open, and I’m like, ‘Well, think about the psychological effect that that has on your teenage child to say such a thing.’”

“I think there’s an enormous social pressure, especially on young males to become taller,” Raimann says. He says some boys perceive the risk of remaining short as greater than the risk of taking experimental drugs.

Zak explains why he feels he has to keep improving. “I’m trying to maximize every aspect of my body. No matter what I do, I still feel like it’s not enough,” he says. And when it comes to girls, he says, “They constantly want something better.”

Across social media, short men lament poor treatment romantically, pointing to research on the advantages taller men enjoy both professionally and in dating. On Reddit, communities like r/short and r/shortguys draw tens of thousands of members sharing their experiences. One user, who says he is a 21-year-old in Spain, tells me in a DM that reassuring stories about other short men did little to change his outlook.

“People know how a short person is treated in this world; the problem is they try to turn a blind eye. They play dumb, saying things like: ‘Well, but I know someone who…’ — purely anecdotal experiences that honestly don’t reflect the reality for the majority.”

For all of the recent talk of short kings in pop culture, the men I spoke with describe familiar stigmas around male height.

Jason Nagata, a pediatrician specializing in adolescent and young adult medicine who treats patients with eating disorders, recently heard through consultations about a patient asking to use erda to try to get taller. Nagata says the repetition of certain types of content can distort a young person’s sense of how common these practices are.

“I do think that social media and online communities normalize behaviors that might otherwise seem extreme,” Nagata says. “So if you’re constantly seeing peers or influencers discussing hormones, drugs, steroids, or surgery as sort of ordinary optimization tools, then it makes it seem like everyone’s doing that.” A young man who engages with this content gets more of it in his feed, he says. “So I think you can have a misperception of what’s normal.”

Nagata says that one way to help dissuade this kind of behavior is to hear kids out. “When talking with teens about height or other appearance concerns, I recommend starting with open-ended, nonjudgmental conversations,” he adds. “Parents can lead with curiosity and try to understand what their child is concerned about, what they hope to achieve, and what they have heard or seen online. Once you understand where they’re coming from, you’re in a better position to provide helpful, evidence-based guidance.”

Zak says he first started looking into steroids and looksmaxxing drugs when he was 12. He remembers a teacher catching him researching performance-enhancing drugs on his school Chromebook. “My friend has a video of my teacher yelling at me,” he says.

The pandemic put his interest in pharmacology into overdrive, as he was able to spend hours online doing research. “I have photos of my screen time. It’s literally 17 hours of YouTube videos on this stuff,” he says of the period. “I was obsessed. I forgot to eat my meals.” He tells me he even performed nipple-reduction surgery on himself after using YouTube to watch surgical procedures.

Asked why he shares his experiments online, Zak says, “I just want to show other people how it’s so possible to literally do anything.” He describes commenters under his erda posts announcing that their own orders will arrive in a few weeks and asking whether the side effects are as bad as they sound. He says he does not sell erdafitinib or give out his source. He also thinks the size of an online audience can give a misleading impression of how many people are actually taking it.

“You would think that there’s a lot of people, but that’s just because having a platform helps you reach so many people.”

A TikTok U.S. spokesperson says the platform prohibits content promoting erda or showing its use, as part of its rules against selling or facilitating access to regulated or high-risk goods. The spokesperson says TikTok may limit search results for unapproved or potentially unsafe products and direct users to authoritative health resources, and that the company continually refines those measures.

Many of the accounts I’d initially seen have since been banned. Right after our interview, Zak sent me an email letting me know his account had been banned, pointing me to his new backup username.

Beyond social platforms, the search for drugs leads to gray-market vendors. Zak tells me he lost money twice trying to buy another compound using Bitcoin. One of his suppliers, he says, worked at a biotech lab.

“I went on a Chinese dating app in a certain city in China that’s known for its biotech labs and things like that,” he says. The woman he met there sent him research chemicals and could even supply custom compounds, he says.

Tim Mackey, whose company S3 Research monitors online drug markets, had his analysts look into erdafitinib after I contacted him. They found discussions on Telegram and other platforms about sourcing and taking the drug. Some people appeared to be buying raw ingredients rather than a finished medicine. Mackey says buyers cannot assume they are getting what is advertised.

“Cancer drugs tend to be in a very controlled supply chain,” he says. What buyers find online could be legitimate medicine diverted from that chain, raw pharmaceutical ingredients not intended for human use, or counterfeit products.

Dauber cautions that the published reports of children growing on erda also describe abnormal bone growth and development. Even so, the warnings haven’t deterred Zak or James. Both say they’re treated better by their peers now that they’re taller. Zak says critics in his comments tell him that he’s trying to die early by taking experimental compounds, but he insists the opposite. He wants to live his life fully and believes the drugs can help him do that. Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Trump's Bizarre Journey Through the Stages of Grief as Democrats Dominated the Midterms Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback As Nicki Minaj Rallied for Trump's GOP, Her Lawyers Told Court She Still Owes Them $295,000

James tells me he is scared of dying and worries about cancer each time he takes a new untested substance. He also says another hospital stay wouldn’t persuade him to stop; he wants to keep going until he reaches a height he is happy with. Somewhere around six foot four. I ask what he imagines life would feel like at that height.

“I don’t know. I feel like I wouldn’t have to worry about anything really, because my entire life, everything that’s made me sad and depressed and just not doing OK, it all stems from just my looks and being insecure, all of that,” he says. “So if I fix everything, almost all my problems would go away. When you’re six-four and you look perfect, your perfect face, perfect everything.”

#3366. Apple recently notified users in 99 countries of potential mercenary spyware attacks

Apple reportedly sent notifications to users in 99 countries warning of potential mercenary spyware attacks, as German authorities investigate reports that lawmakers and government officials may have been targeted. Here are the details.

A couple of reports from The Financial Times and TechCrunch today offer complementary details about a new wave of Apple threat notifications warning users that they may have been targeted by mercenary spyware.

As we’ve covered before, Apple periodically sends out threat notifications to users it believes may have been targeted by mercenary spyware attacks. The company doesn’t disclose who may be behind the attacks or confirm whether a device has been compromised, but advises recipients to take the warnings seriously and seek expert assistance.

You can learn more about Apple’s recommendations for protecting against mercenary spyware, including how to enable Lockdown Mode, here.

Back to today’s reports, The Financial Times says that German lawmakers and government officials began receiving threat notifications from Apple last Thursday, prompting the country’s Federal Office for Information Security to issue an urgent warning over the weekend.

The agency advised recipients to “assume their device is no longer secure,” while the German government said it was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously” and “working flat out to investigate the circumstances of the incident.”

The FT noted that German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius declined to say whether Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those affected, and added that the attacks reportedly exploited a “zero-click” vulnerability, allowing attackers to compromise devices without any interaction.

Knowledge of their targets’ phone numbers was all that the hackers needed to carry out the attack.

As it reported on the alerts, TechCrunch noted that “others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple,” including Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, who shared his alert on X.

It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries.

Mortada also noted in his tweet that he had previously been targeted by Pegasus spyware in 2017 and 2021, and that he does not know who was behind the latest attempt or whether it was connected to an investigative documentary he directed.

Many travelers have learned the hard way that certain cell phone plans can kill your wallet with roaming charges come the end of a trip. This is because your home carrier essentially rents network access from foreign providers if you switch on your data, make a call, or send a text in another country.

However, if you travel often, you don’t need to deal with massive roaming charges at the end of every trip abroad. Certain carriers offer wireless plans with large international data packages included, which means you won’t need to worry about purchasing an international pass or an eSIM while planning your trip. Just touch down and continue using your phone (and your own number) like you would at home.

Ahead are three of the best wireless plans for traveling abroad, including options from T-Mobile, Google Fi, and Verizon.

One of the best cell phone plans for international travel is T-Mobile’s Experience Beyond 2.0 plan. The premium cell package offers unlimited text and 15 gigabytes of high-speed data in more than 215 countries and destinations — all without requiring a separate pass or payment. If you’re traveling to Mexico or Canada, you’ll get 30 gigabytes of data. Once you hit that data cap, you’ll still be able to access the internet, but speeds will slow down a bit. The Experience Beyond plan also comes with other travel perks like hotel and rental car discounts, cruise credits, and even a complimentary drink on Delta flights. #3363. SCOTUS sets hearing date for Apple’s appeal in Epic Games case

The U.S. Supreme Court has officially scheduled oral arguments in Apple’s appeal in its long-running legal battle with Epic Games. Here are the details.

Back in 2020, Epic Games sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store for introducing an alternative in-app payment system through a remotely activated update.

The following year, despite ruling in Apple’s favor on nine of Epic’s ten claims, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled that Apple could no longer prevent developers from directing users to alternative payment options outside the App Store.

As a result, Apple changed its rules to allow external purchase links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on transactions completed through them, along with restrictions on how those links could be presented.

Epic challenged Apple’s implementation, and the district court agreed. In April 2025, Judge Rogers ordered Apple to remove those restrictions and stop charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store, finding the company in civil contempt for violating the original injunction.

Since then, Apple has allowed developers to direct users to external payment options in the US App Store without charging a commission, while continuing to challenge the contempt ruling.

After unsuccessful attempts before the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, Apple eventually took its case to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to review whether Apple could be held in contempt for violating the “spirit” of an injunction, even when its text did not specifically prohibit the conduct in question.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only review the civil contempt ruling, not how much, if anything, Apple can charge developers for purchases made outside the App Store. That issue is being handled separately by the district court, after the Ninth Circuit overturned the blanket ban on commissions in December.

Earlier today, the Supreme Court’s official docket for the case was updated with a date for oral arguments.

According to the filing, Apple and Epic Games will present their arguments before the Supreme Court on Monday, January 11, 2027, though both sides have already outlined many of their arguments in recent filings.

In September, Apple filed its opening brief with the Supreme Court, arguing that the contempt ruling should be overturned because the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from charging commissions on purchases made outside the App Store.

In its brief, Apple cited multiple court decisions to support its argument that a party cannot be held in civil contempt unless an injunction clearly prohibits the conduct in question.

A few days after Apple’s filing, the US Department of Justice and several legal and business groups also submitted briefs supporting at least part of the company’s argument.

The DOJ, however, also argued that the lower courts were right to hold Apple in contempt over some of its restrictions on external purchase links, including a requirement that developers use what Apple called “plain buttons,” which could not have contrasting backgrounds.

With the hearing now scheduled, the case is one step closer to a final decision from the Supreme Court. However, both sides still have some paperwork to submit before then, as Epic Games has until November 13 to file its brief responding to Apple’s arguments, while Apple’s reply is due December 14.

#3360. Apple earnings suggest the iPhone 18 launch strategy is really working

Yesterday’s AAPL earnings report revealed record revenue for a September quarter, and within it was an arguably even more significant record: iPhone revenue.

That’s because this year’s quarter only includes just two new iPhone models compared to the four released last year …

Apple reported fiscal quarter four revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year. Within that was iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, which was also a quarterly record. What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

#3359. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3358. Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

What’s your take? Please share in the comments.

#3356. New iPad mini hands-on: Refreshed design, OLED display, more

Apple’s smallest iPad has gotten its biggest update in years. The new iPad mini features a much thinner and lighter design, a larger OLED display, water resistance, and the powerful A20 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing the new iPad mini, and there’s a lot to like — but also a couple of frustrations. Here’s everything you need to know.

The new iPad mini lives up to the “mini” name even more than its predecessor. It’s significantly thinner, down from 6.3mm on the previous iPad mini to 5.4mm on the new model. In fact, that puts it very close to the ultra-thin iPad Pro and the unfolded iPhone Duo. Here’s how it compares:

The new iPad mini is also significantly lighter, dropping from 293 grams to 255 grams. That puts it in the realm of the iPhone Duo, for comparison’s sake:

The reduction in weight and thickness was immediately noticeable when I picked up the new iPad mini. It feels significantly nicer to hold, more premium, and less “dense” in my hands.

The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch screen, a slight increase from the previous generation’s 8.3-inch display. The overall footprint is mostly the same (the new model is actually about 2.2mm narrower). The larger screen is possible because the new iPad mini’s bezels are 24 percent thinner than before.

In addition to allowing a bigger screen in the same form factor, the narrower bezels also modernize the iPad mini’s overall look and feel. The bezels are noticeably slimmer than the iPad Air and base model iPad, and slightly thinner than the iPad Pro.

With smaller bezels, a thinner chassis, and a lighter weight, the new iPad mini feels significantly more premium than before. It reminds me less of the base model iPad or iPad Air and more of the iPad Pro, just shrunken down.

The big news about the display, though, is the switch to OLED. This marks Apple’s first non-Pro iPad to offer an OLED screen. It’s not the fancy tandem OLED display of the iPad Pro, but it’s a huge improvement over the previous model’s LCD panel.

The new iPad mini offers SDR brightness up to 600 nits, up from the previous model’s 500 nits max. The iPad mini also supports HDR content, with up to 1200 nits peak brightness.

The new iPad mini’s screen is undeniably an improvement over its predecessor. All of the inherent benefits of OLED apply here, including better colors, improved contrast, higher brightness, and more.

Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind. Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.

Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering significantly faster pixel response time than the previous generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother scrolling and reduced motion blur.

I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages, scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher refresh-rate display.

I’m sure Apple knows the iPad mini’s market, and it seems to have decided not to prioritize ProMotion based on that information. However, as someone who has longed for a so-called “iPad mini Pro” for years, I’m disappointed by the decision. The new iPad mini’s screen is so much better … I just wish Apple had gone that extra step and added ProMotion. We’ve reached a point where ProMotion should be table stakes, especially after Apple brought it to the base iPhone 17 last year.

For an extra $100, you can upgrade the new iPad mini to have a nano-texture display (on the 256GB and 512GB models).

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s nano-texture display and have it on my 14-inch MacBook Pro. On the iPad mini, I think it makes even more sense.

The iPad mini is ultra-portable, and you naturally carry it around and use it in different lighting environments. The nano-texture glass helps reduce reflections and glare in a wide variety of lighting conditions. I also really like the combination of the iPad mini’s book-like size and the nano-texture finish.

There is a slight tradeoff in color vibrancy compared to a glossy OLED screen, as on other Apple devices with nano-texture, but it’s a very minor difference in my experience. The screen still looks fantastic.

One of the more interesting changes with the new iPad mini is something Apple calls the “Acoustic Display.” Instead of traditional speakers with visible grilles, Apple has developed a new system that uses the display itself to produce sound.

Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s significantly thinner design.

In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a test bed of sorts.)

The Acoustic Display also plays an important role in another major upgrade: water and dust resistance. The new iPad mini is IP67 rated, which means it can be immersed in 1 meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. It’s the first iPad to have an official water-resistance rating.

Adding water resistance to the iPad mini is particularly notable given its size and portability. I naturally find myself wanting to take it everywhere, and water resistance makes that more feasible.

One use case where all these improvements really come together is reading. The thinner and lighter design, nano-texture glass, and water resistance make the new iPad mini the most compelling iPad yet to serve as an e-reader.

The new iPad mini is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which I already covered in detail in my iPhone 18 Pro review. The short version: the A20 Pro chip gives you plenty of power for anything you can throw at the iPad mini today.

One detail worth calling out is that Apple uses two different versions of the A20 Pro in the iPad mini. The 128GB and 256GB models feature a five-core CPU and 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512GB model gets a six-core CPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. All three configurations feature the same seven-core GPU.

I don’t think anyone should buy the 512GB version of the iPad mini just for those extra cores. You should pick your iPad mini configuration based on how much storage you need, not the version of the A20 Pro chip. You don’t need to worry about performance with the new iPad mini. And perhaps most importantly, the A20 Pro chip ensures the iPad mini has enough headroom for the future.

There’s been a lot of consternation about where the iPad mini fits in a world where the iPhone Duo also now exists. It’s a fair question. After all, when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, the two devices share a similar form factor … but that’s really where the similarities end.

The iPad mini offers the full-fledged, unapologetic iPadOS experience. It supports the full multitasking prowess of an iPad Pro, including windowing and the menu bar. The new iPad mini also supports extended display mode, so you can plug it into an external display and extend your iPad experience there.

The iPad mini also gets iPadOS app layouts, and most importantly, a desktop-class browsing experience in Safari. It’s a remarkably capable device in a remarkably compact form factor. It fits where other iPads can’t, yet it runs the same version of iPadOS as other iPads.

The new iPad mini does all of that, but better than before. The thinner, lighter design paired with smaller bezels gives the new iPad mini a meaningful visual refresh. The added water resistance means you can do even more with the compact and pocketable iPad mini design.

But all of this comes at a higher price of $699. This marks the second price increase for the iPad mini this year. It started the year at $499, rose to $599 as part of Apple’s broader price increases in June, and is now $699 as of this refresh.

The new iPad mini also still starts with 128GB of storage. Increasing the base storage to 256GB would’ve helped ease some of the pain of that price increase. It’s also getting increasingly hard to manage a device with 128GB, particularly with the storage needs of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. The lack of ProMotion and Face ID also make the price increase sting more.

Ultimately, the iPad mini form factor is a joy to use. The design feels great in the hand, and having the full iPadOS experience in such a compact device remains impressive. It’s not quite the “iPad mini Pro” I’ve always wanted, but it’s big upgrade to a form factor that I’ve always loved.

#3354. Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

Apple argued that the touchscreen isn’t the headline feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, merely a bonus.

The headline should instead be the quality of the display itself – with the company effectively suggesting that the $400 premium is positively cheap for what you’re getting …

Apple published a white paper in which it argues that the latest MacBook Pro display is essentially a smaller version of its professional reference monitor, the Studio Display XDR.

$400 for the screen and new design isn’t my issue, my issue is the cost of storage and memory. $600 more to go from 24gb to 48gb or nearly a grand for 64gb. You can easily spend nearly double the cost of the machine just getting it to a semi-future proof spec.

Given that this costs anywhere from $2,899 to $3,599 just for a display (albeit a significantly larger one with a correspondingly higher resolution), this does put into perspective that $400 extra over the MacBook Pro with the standard screen. Here’s what Apple has to say about it:

PROLED XDR display, the best display in a pro laptop, finally overcomes these historic limitations. For the first time, a MacBook Pro display uses tandem OLED technology, delivering up to 1000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, 2000 nits of peak high dynamic range (HDR) and standard dynamic range (SDR) brightness, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with accurate, per-pixel black levels.

It’s driven in real time by an all-new display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates each pixel for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions—delivering creative precision out of the box and protecting panel lifespan over time. And a unique manufacturing process ensures panel-to-panel consistency and minimizes off-axis color shift, a first for any OLED laptop.

As Macworld spotted, that’s almost identical to the company’s description of the the Studio Display XDR.

In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.”

Resolution aside, the other specs are identical with just one exception: the contrast ratio. As for that exception, the MacBook display comes out on top with a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, in contrast with the Studio Display XDR’s one million.

Does this change your own perspective of the price premium of the OLED model? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3351. Channel 4 Cancels ‘Married At First Sight UK’ After Rape Allegations

Channel 4 has canceled Married at First Sight UK (MAFS UK) following two external reviews into welfare on the show that was hit by rape allegations earlier this year.

Despite one review saying “it would be reasonable to continue producing future series,” Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra said MAFS UK has now “run its course.” Neither the current sixth season, which had been filmed, or spin-off Second Marriage at First Sight, which was due to roll cameras over the summer, will air. The previous five seasons will remain absent from Channel 4’s VoD player, although other versions from around the world are available to watch including Married at First Sight U.S. Related Stories News 'The Cube' Creator Adam Adler Joins Channel 4's Production Biz As Creative Director News Disney+ & Channel 4 Strike Landmark Deal In UK

“The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over ten years,” said Dogra, who was mere weeks into the job when the MAFS UK scandal erupted. “Channel 4 has always thrived on reinvention and this is a moment to kickstart a new era of creative renewal, using the considerable budget to find the next generation of distinctive and disruptive British television.” Watch on Deadline

The reviews were commissioned after BBC News published allegations from two women who alleged they were raped by partners they met on the show, while another claimed she was victim of a non-consensual sex act. The three men accused of wrongdoing all deny the accusations. One cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape over the summer.

While Channel 4 said the specific allegations “remain a matter for the relevant authorities,” the first review from legal firm Clyde & Co examined welfare protocols on MAFS UK and whether regulator Ofcom’s code was breached. The second, conducted by ex-BBC One boss Lorraine Heggessey, looked into whether changes should be made to protocols for MAFS UK to strengthen contributor welfare in the future. Separately, Ofcom opened its own investigation in July.

Rules broken around “prohibited substances”

Clyde & Co’s review found Channel 4 and producer CPL Productions had not breached the Ofcom code.

It did, however, “identify a small number of instances in which the show’s established protocols had not been fully applied.”

These, it said, related to contributors breaking the rules around “prohibited substances.” These contributors were given a “first and final warning” rather than “being removed from the progamme,” according to the review.

Clyde & Co, which examined more than 30,000 documents, 20 hours of broadcast and unbroadcast footage and conducted 15 interviews, said CPL and Channel 4 could have “undertaken a more structured longer-term review over multiple series so that any further tightening of processes and procedures could be made in response to a more holistic and long-term assessment.”

Heggessey’s forward-facing review, meanwhile, suggested Channel 4 could make more MAFS UK with various welfare tweaks, although Dogra, who once again said today she is “very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt,” came to a different view.

Notably, Heggessey said that while “the complexity of the production” requires “significant oversight from Channel 4,” the network’s involvement has “at times led to a lack of objective scrutiny over some production decisions.”

Heggessey’s recommendations included separate bedrooms on couples’ wedding nights and honeymoons before giving them the option to “opt in” to sharing a room, reviewing the frequency with which they are asked about the physical side of their relationship by the production team and reducing the number of couples per series.

Within the couples’ apartments, Heggessey suggested Channel 4 could install CCTV, use individual safe words and panic buttons, and provide lockable ensuite bathrooms.

She also suggested various tweaks to casting including “undertaking psychological testing and profiling of final contributors in person rather than via video call,” alongside considering whether psychological assessments should “take into account current societal trends” like misogyny and attitudes to consent.

As it stands, these recommendations will not be taken up as the show has been axed. Instead, new Channel 4 programs chief David Brindley, who begins in January, will be looking after MAFS UK’s reallocated budget.

“MAFS UK has been enjoyed by millions of viewers, made possible by the willingness of its contributors to embrace the social experiment at the heart of the show and the many talented people involved in its production,” said Dogra. “I am grateful to everyone at Channel 4 and CPL Productions who has worked on the show and want to thank them for their significant efforts to protect the welfare of contributors, something which was recognised in both reviews. I hope our actions – in swiftly commissioning the review and taking clear, decisive steps – demonstrate our commitment to the wellbeing of all contributors and our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards.”

A CPL statement said the indie “understands Channel 4’s decision to bring MAFS to an end.” “The independent reviews gave CPL the opportunity to discuss in depth the welfare processes already in place and that the Heggessey review found that ‘the welfare protocols for MAFS UK were extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard from which other productions in the industry have learnt’,” read the statement. “CPL has always put contributor welfare at the heart of its programme making and will continue to do so. CPL have worked closely with Channel 4 for many years and throughout the review process, and we look forward to working with them again in the future.”

MAFS, which originated in Denmark 13 years ago, remains huge in several territories, with the American, Australian and New Zealand versions all still available on Channel 4’s VoD player. The U.S. version airs on Peacock.

Across a decade, MAFS UK has been a huge hit for Channel 4, moreso when the format was tweaked in 2021 to bring it more in line with other versions like the popular Australian one.

The MAFS UK reviews were at least the third set of external reviews launched by Channel 4 over the past decade, following one into the suicide of true crime producer John Balson and another into the behavior of Escape to the Chateau hosts Dick and Angel Strawbridge. The Balson review found that Channel 4 had acted “reasonably and appropriately” with its duty of care before the producer took his own life. Channel 4 cut ties with the Strawbridges after that review.

#3350. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.
